---
title: "Explaining models"
subtitle: "Examine the words a fitted text model learned to weight"
description: "Learn how to read linear model coefficients and why a plausible explanation can still belong to a weak model."
categories: [model development, explanation, text classification]
---

A reviewer asks why the model gave a paragraph the label modern. She needs to
examine the words that affected its score.

A plausible explanation does not establish model quality. Even a weak model
can produce an apparently convincing coefficient table.

This lesson fits the same model family for two tasks. Grouped folds in lesson
43 placed ridge logistic regression with penalty `0.01` among the leading
candidates. The final test provided separate evaluation evidence. The era
design has useful evaluation evidence, but the party design with these features
and this penalty does not.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

This lesson shows how to:

- extract coefficients from a fitted workflow.
- read positive and negative coefficients in plain language.
- examine terms weighted by an era classifier.
- mask terms from a weak political classifier.
- keep explanation separate from evidence that a model is right.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Fit the era model for inspection

A **coefficient** is a learned weight. In this linear model, a positive
coefficient increases the prediction score for the second class, `1900 or later`.
A negative coefficient increases the score for the first class, `before 1900`.
Coefficient size describes the fitted weight on a tf-idf feature.

This direction depends on outcome order. The shared corpus helper places
`before 1900` first and `1900 or later` second. The second class is the target
of this binary glmnet fit.

Ranking coefficients by raw magnitude does not prove exactly what the model
relied on. The features are correlated, and ridge regression spreads weight
across related words. A different penalty could change the ranking. Read the
list as heavily weighted terms in this fitted model, not as fixed meanings for
historical periods.

glmnet standardizes predictors while fitting but returns coefficients on the
original tf-idf scale. A rare term with little spread can therefore receive a
larger raw coefficient than a common term with the same standardized effect.
Multiplying each coefficient by its feature standard deviation would produce a
different ranking.

The model below uses every paragraph in the corpus. Teams often want
explanations for the final model they deploy after training on all available
data. This full-corpus fit therefore has no evaluation score.

The evaluation lesson's 0.8457 repeated-holdout mean describes different fits.
Those models used three quarters of the speeches for training and the rest for
evaluation. This page does not measure the performance of the full-corpus
model. Similar-looking coefficients could occur in either a strong or weak fit.

The folds selected the model family and penalty before this refit. Refitting on
all rows changes the exact coefficients, so the table explains the refitted
model rather than reproducing the coefficients from any one fold.

```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tibble)
  library(stringr)
  library(recipes)
  library(textrecipes)
  library(parsnip)
  library(workflows)
  library(broom)
  library(glmnet)
})

source("R/inaugural-corpus.R")
paragraphs <- inaugural_paragraphs()

make_text_workflow <- function(formula, training_data) {
  recipe(formula, data = training_data) |>
    step_tokenize(paragraph) |>
    step_stopwords(paragraph) |>
    step_tokenfilter(paragraph, max_tokens = 500) |>
    step_tfidf(paragraph) |>
    workflow() |>
    add_model(
      logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 0) |>
        set_engine("glmnet")
    )
}

set.seed(4500)
era_fitted <- make_text_workflow(era ~ paragraph, paragraphs) |>
  fit(data = paragraphs)

era_coefficients <- tidy(extract_fit_parsnip(era_fitted)) |>
  mutate(
    word = str_remove(term, "^tfidf_paragraph_"),
    direction = if_else(estimate >= 0, "1900 or later", "before 1900")
  )

check_words <- c("attention", "object", "effect", "placed", "parts", "opinion")
checked_coefficients <- era_coefficients |>
  filter(word %in% check_words) |>
  arrange(word)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  checked_coefficients |>
    select(word, estimate, direction) |>
    mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 2)),
  col.names = c("Term", "Coefficient", "Class with increased score"),
  caption = "Selected large era-model coefficients",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(paragraphs), 1377L),
  identical(n_distinct(paragraphs$president), 40L),
  identical(levels(paragraphs$era), c("before 1900", "1900 or later")),
  identical(nrow(era_coefficients), 501L),
  identical(sort(checked_coefficients$word), sort(check_words)),
  all(abs(checked_coefficients$estimate) > 7),
  identical(
    checked_coefficients$direction,
    rep("before 1900", length(check_words))
  )
)
```

The fitted era model has `r nrow(era_coefficients)` terms. This count includes the
intercept, the constant term. The listed words increase the score for
`before 1900` in this fit. They are
formal-register signals in this corpus, not summaries of what any period was
about.

## Read both directions

The largest positive coefficients increase the score for `1900 or later`.
The largest negative coefficients increase the score for `before 1900`.
This table describes fitted weights rather than word meanings.

```{r}
era_extremes <- bind_rows(
  era_coefficients |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    slice_max(estimate, n = 8) |>
    arrange(desc(estimate)),
  era_coefficients |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    slice_min(estimate, n = 8) |>
    arrange(estimate)
) |>
  mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 2)) |>
  select(word, direction, estimate)

sensitive_terms <- c("slavery", "slave", "race", "war")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  era_extremes,
  col.names = c("Term", "Class with increased score", "Coefficient"),
  caption = "Strongest positive and negative coefficients in the era model",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(era_extremes), 16L),
  max(era_extremes$estimate) > 8,
  min(era_extremes$estimate) < -15,
  all(era_extremes$direction %in% levels(paragraphs$era)),
  !any(str_to_lower(era_extremes$word) %in% sensitive_terms)
)
```

With all other features unchanged, a larger tf-idf value on a positive term
increases the score for `1900 or later`. A larger value on a negative term
increases the score for `before 1900`. The linear model adds these weighted
contributions.

## Explain the weak model too

The party model did not improve on the deployable largest-class rule at the
paragraph or speech split. Its balanced accuracy was near chance. The same
extraction code still produces coefficients. A clear coefficient table
therefore does not establish that a model is useful.

```{r}
study <- read_csv(
  "data/inaugural/split-study.csv",
  na = c("", "NA"),
  col_types = cols(
    task = col_character(),
    split_scheme = col_character(),
    replicate = col_integer(),
    accuracy = col_double(),
    bal_accuracy = col_double(),
    train_majority_accuracy = col_double(),
    test_majority_rate = col_double(),
    length_rule_accuracy = col_double(),
    test_rows = col_integer(),
    test_speeches = col_integer()
  )
)

party_rows <- paragraphs |>
  filter(party %in% c("Democratic", "Republican")) |>
  mutate(party = factor(party))

set.seed(4503)
party_fitted <- make_text_workflow(party ~ paragraph, party_rows) |>
  fit(data = party_rows)

party_coefficients <- tidy(extract_fit_parsnip(party_fitted)) |>
  mutate(
    word = str_remove(term, "^tfidf_paragraph_"),
    direction = if_else(estimate >= 0, levels(party_rows$party)[2], levels(party_rows$party)[1])
  )

party_extremes <- party_coefficients |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  slice_max(abs(estimate), n = 10) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate))) |>
  mutate(
    term = paste("term", row_number()),
    estimate = round(estimate, 2)
  ) |>
  select(term, direction, estimate)

party_summary <- study |>
  filter(task == "party") |>
  summarise(
    mean_accuracy = mean(accuracy),
    mean_bal_accuracy = mean(bal_accuracy),
    mean_train_majority = mean(train_majority_accuracy),
    .by = split_scheme
  )

party_paragraph <- party_summary |>
  filter(split_scheme == "paragraph")
party_speech <- party_summary |>
  filter(split_scheme == "speech")
party_president <- party_summary |>
  filter(split_scheme == "president")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  party_extremes,
  col.names = c("Masked term", "Class with increased score", "Coefficient"),
  caption = "Large coefficients from the party model that did not pass evaluation",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(party_rows), 1197L),
  identical(n_distinct(party_rows$president), 31L),
  identical(nrow(party_coefficients), 501L),
  identical(nrow(party_extremes), 10L),
  identical(party_extremes$term, paste("term", 1:10)),
  !any(party_extremes$term %in% party_coefficients$word),
  identical(round(party_paragraph$mean_accuracy, 4), 0.6060),
  identical(round(party_paragraph$mean_train_majority, 4), 0.6067),
  identical(round(party_speech$mean_accuracy, 4), 0.5514),
  identical(round(party_speech$mean_train_majority, 4), 0.6563),
  identical(round(party_president$mean_accuracy, 4), 0.4997),
  identical(round(party_president$mean_bal_accuracy, 4), 0.5090),
  max(abs(party_coefficients$estimate)) > 13
)
```

The lesson deliberately withholds party terms. The model scores
`r round(party_speech$mean_accuracy, 4)` at the speech split against a deployable
baseline of `r round(party_speech$mean_train_majority, 4)`. Its person-split
balanced accuracy is `r round(party_president$mean_bal_accuracy, 4)`.

Displaying the terms could encourage political interpretations that the model's
evaluation does not justify. Masking preserves the teaching point. The table
can look convincing even when the model performs poorly.

## What to remember

- A coefficient is a learned weight that affects the score for a class.
- Coefficients show fitted weights after preprocessing, not proof of causation.
- A coefficient is not proof that the model is right.
- The era explanation matters because the era model performed better than simple baselines.
- The party explanation is a warning because this model did not learn party.

If the score fails, the explanation should make you more cautious, not more
comfortable.
